Week 70: Patronage, Voting, and Public Myth

Executive protection, weaker voting safeguards, and leader-centered commemoration advanced together while courts and lawmakers offered only partial resistance.

Week 70 was shaped less by shock than by arrangement. Power was not seized in one gesture. It was sorted, routed, and made easier to use for friends and harder to resist for others. The week’s most important acts joined legal protection, public money, electoral control, and public symbolism in one broad pattern. Each move had its own file, hearing, or ceremony. Together, they showed a state more willing to serve the ruler’s needs first.

At the close of the last period, the Democracy Clock stood at 8:13 p.m. By the end of Week 70, it stood at 8:14 p.m., a net shift of 0.2 minutes. The movement was small because resistance still appeared in courts and in parts of Congress. It moved forward because the week’s strongest actions were structural. The Justice Department opened a new channel for executive-controlled payouts, legal protection was extended to the president and his circle, voting-rights barriers weakened, and public commemoration was bent toward personal and sacred display.

The clearest development came from the Justice Department. It created a $1.776 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund after Trump dropped his IRS lawsuit. At nearly the same moment, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche barred the government from pursuing tax-related claims against Trump, his family, and affiliated companies. These were not stray favors. They joined public money and legal immunity in one package.

The winners were plain. Trump, his relatives, allied claimants, and executive officers who wanted broad control over settlement money all gained room to act. The losers were just as plain: equal enforcement, ordinary taxpayers, and the idea that the law binds the officeholder before it serves him. A government that can both pay favored people and waive future scrutiny for the president has crossed from selective indulgence toward formal protection.

Opacity deepened the damage. Blanche and the fund’s backers gave conflicting accounts of whether payouts would be publicly disclosed. Senate Democrats pressed him in appropriations hearings and questioned the legal basis for the arrangement. House Democrats filed an amicus brief challenging any settlement tied to the IRS suit. The fight was not only about money. It was about whether executive spending could be hidden inside settlement language and then defended as routine.

Resistance came quickly, though not cleanly. Bipartisan lawmakers drafted bills to block the fund. Senate Republicans revolted against it and stalled related legislation. Two January 6 officers sued Trump, Blanche, and Scott Bessent over the agreement, while Senate Judiciary Democrats demanded preservation of the records behind it. A judge dismissed Trump’s withdrawn IRS case, underscoring that the courts still controlled their own docket. But the deeper fact remained. The executive had already shown how legal machinery could be turned into patronage and self-protection before oversight could catch up.

A second development unfolded through election law and election administration. The Supreme Court weakened protections for Black-majority districts under the Voting Rights Act. That ruling did not stay abstract for long. South Carolina’s governor called a special legislative session on congressional redistricting, opening a fast path to redraw representation in ways critics said would weaken Black voting power. Doctrine moved first. State action followed at once.

North Carolina supplied the administrative side of the same story. Its board of elections prepared to vote on a new set of rules defended in the language of integrity and attacked as suppressive. That language mattered. It showed how restriction now travels under the sign of fairness, and how the burden of proof shifts onto those who fear exclusion. The state does not need to say it wants fewer disfavored voters. It can say it wants cleaner rolls, safer systems, and more trust.

The winners here were mapmakers, partisan election managers, and those who benefit when access is narrowed without open disfranchisement. The losers were Black voters, communities already forced to fight for representation, and the older federal promise that voting-rights law would do more than bless procedure after the fact. Federal judges in Maine and Wisconsin did dismiss Justice Department suits seeking detailed voter data, and the administration’s effort to cast voting machines as national-security risks failed. Those checks mattered. They did not erase the week’s main direction.

Civil society answered in the old way. Thousands gathered in Selma and Montgomery to defend voting rights. Their presence did not change the rulings or halt the state plans. But it marked the line between formal legality and democratic consent. Week 70 showed how quickly a national rollback can become local practice, and how protest now often arrives after the ground has already shifted.

A third development concerned memory, ceremony, and the use of public symbols. The administration took control of America250 planning and redirected funds toward Freedom 250. Government organizers and allied speakers then staged the Rededicate 250 event, promoting a Christian nationalist account of the nation’s founding. This was not mere pageantry. It was an attempt to place official blessing on a narrowed story of who the country is and what its past means.

The same pattern appeared in stone and steel. The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts approved the design for Trump’s triumphal arch in Washington. Trump also held a press event at the site of his planned Golden Ballroom. Reports on his golf travel showed large taxpayer costs. These acts differed in scale, but not in kind. Public office, public money, and public attention were repeatedly drawn toward the leader’s image, his monuments, and his private grandeur.

Money ran through this symbolic project as well. Freedom 250 solicited corporate sponsorship tied to access to Trump. That turned a public commemoration into a donor channel. The winners were sponsors, insiders, and the political culture that treats access as a thing to buy. The losers were the civic idea of a national anniversary shared across factions, and the boundary between public celebration and private influence. In Week 70, history was not only retold. It was packaged, sold, and tied to the ruler’s presence.

This mattered because symbolic power is not soft power when it is backed by appropriations, official platforms, and design bodies. A state ceremony can teach obedience as surely as a rule can. A monument can outlast a hearing. When religion, founding myth, and personal glorification are fused in public ritual, the state is not only remembering the nation. It is instructing the nation whom to revere.

A fourth development centered on immigration enforcement. The Department of Homeland Security required many green card applicants to apply from their home countries, making status adjustment harder and more disruptive. The administration continued large-scale raids that a study said did not help native-born workers. Texas officials placed buoys along the Rio Grande near Eagle Pass. The CDC suspended entry of certain non-U.S. citizens from Ebola-affected countries for thirty days. These were separate tools. They worked in the same direction: harder entry, harder status, harder safety.

The human cost was documented in blunt terms. California reported severe overcrowding, poor care, and abuse in ICE detention facilities. A Brookings report said more than 145,000 children in the United States had experienced parental detention under current enforcement. North Carolina groups rallied against detention expansion. A Chicago alderperson sued over alleged assault and detention by federal agents at a hospital. The state’s coercive reach was visible not only at the border, but in courts, clinics, and homes.

Courts intervened, though unevenly. A federal judge in New York barred ICE from making routine arrests in or around three Manhattan immigration courthouses, protecting access to hearings. Judge Birotte stayed ICE guidance that had rescinded victim-centered enforcement policies. A judge found that ICE agents in Oregon had likely made unlawful warrantless arrests of farm workers using facial recognition. An ICE officer in Minnesota was charged over the shooting of a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown. These were real checks. They were also case by case.

The limits of those checks were visible too. A federal appeals court upheld a ruling that kept Mahmoud Khalil detained and eligible for deportation. The week therefore did not show a simple story of executive escalation or judicial rescue. It showed immigration as a field where unequal status is enforced through many small levers, while relief depends on scattered plaintiffs, narrow rulings, and the luck of forum. The winners were enforcement agencies and officials who could still impose fear and disruption at scale. The losers were migrants, mixed-status families, and the promise that due process should not depend on endurance alone.

A fifth development lay in the overlap between private gain and public power. Reports showed that Trump and his advisers made thousands of stock trades without a qualified blind trust. Other reporting tied stock purchases to later or same-day public praise of Apple, Dell, Micron, and Thermo Fisher. The administration also launched TrumpRx and a Medicare pilot expanding access to GLP-1 obesity drugs, a policy that could benefit companies linked to the president’s investments. None of this required a single smoking gun. The pattern itself was the fact.

Donor influence sharpened the same picture. Reynolds American gave $5 million to Trump’s super PAC before a favorable vape policy change. Freedom 250 offered sponsor access to Trump. Trump retaliated against Republicans who pushed for release of Epstein-related files, signaling that even demands for disclosure inside his own party could bring punishment. The winners were donors, firms, and insiders able to move close to the line where policy and portfolio meet. The losers were fair dealing, public trust, and any clear claim that executive choices were being made at arm’s length from private interest.

This development was distinct from the Justice Department story, though the two reinforced each other. One concerned immunity and public payouts. The other concerned enrichment, access, and the market value of proximity to power. Together they showed a governing style in which office, money, and favor no longer needed careful separation. They could travel on the same track.

A sixth development concerned Congress and the fragility of its checks. The Senate advanced a war powers resolution to curb Trump’s Iran operations, asserting its constitutional role over military action. The Department of Defense inspector general also opened an inquiry into U.S. airstrikes during Operation Southern Spear. These were signs that some parts of the system still tried to mark limits. They mattered because war powers are among the hardest powers to reclaim once habit is lost.

Yet the same week showed how easily those checks can be delayed. House Republican leaders pulled a vote on a war powers resolution over Iran, shielding the president from a direct floor test. Trump called for Senate Republicans to replace the Senate parliamentarian, pressing an internal legislative referee to align with his goals. Earlier, the parliamentarian had stripped a ballroom spending provision from a DHS bill, showing that procedure could still bite. But the president’s answer was not accommodation. It was pressure on the gatekeeper.

The winners in this struggle were leadership figures who could decide whether oversight would ripen into action at all. The losers were rank-and-file legislators, constitutional balance, and the idea that internal referees should be free from presidential command. Week 70 did not show Congress wholly surrendered. It showed a rise-and-retreat pattern: assertion in one chamber, withdrawal in another, and constant pressure on the weak joints of procedure.

A seventh development came from the courts, which remained the main active brake on overreach but not a steady one. Judge Bates ordered the White House and the vice president’s office to comply with the Presidential Records Act, preserving the paper trail on which future oversight depends. Judge Crenshaw dismissed the indictment against Kilmar Ábrego García as vindictive prosecution. Federal prosecutors in Chicago dropped the remaining charges against the Broadview Six after misconduct findings. These were strong acts. They said that records must be kept, retaliation has limits, and tainted protest cases can still collapse under scrutiny.

Other rulings reinforced the same point in narrower ways. Courts kept protections in place for transgender plaintiffs facing transfer and treatment changes, and for providers of gender-affirming care for minors. A judge denied a partial stay in one case against the administration, while the D.C. Circuit later granted an administrative stay pending appeal. The New York Times sued the Pentagon over a revised press access policy, opening another lane of review. Routine judicial gatekeeping also appeared in criminal and appellate cases outside the week’s main political fights. Ordinary law still functioned in many rooms.

But the brake was uneven. Relief was often temporary, plaintiff-bound, or vulnerable on appeal. Trial courts could act sharply; higher courts could narrow that relief in days. The winners were those with access to counsel, time, and a court willing to hear them. The losers were broader publics who cannot litigate every abuse one case at a time. Judicial review still worked. It did not yet amount to a full counterforce.

An eighth and final development tied immigration enforcement to campus dissent through a common method: surveillance joined to retaliation. In Oregon, a judge found that ICE agents had likely made unlawful warrantless arrests of farm workers using facial recognition. At the University of Michigan, a student sued over alleged surveillance and retaliation tied to Gaza protests, claiming that monitoring and false reports had been used to burden a protester through formal process. These were different institutions. The mechanism was similar.

That mechanism matters. Surveillance need not end in conviction to chill conduct. It can sort targets, raise costs, and teach others what scrutiny feels like. In immigration, it widened the reach of enforcement into ordinary life. On campus, it threatened the space where dissent is supposed to be tested rather than tracked. The winners were institutions able to gather information and turn it into leverage. The losers were farm workers, students, and the habit of speaking or assembling without fear that every act will be stored, matched, and used later.

One other thread ran quietly beneath the week’s louder conflicts. Administrative life did not stop. Agencies still issued notices, held advisory meetings, and moved routine rules. A terrorism case proceeded through ordinary federal court channels. Those facts mattered. They showed that formal legality had not vanished. But the deeper lesson was that ordinary process can survive even as its purpose shifts, and that expert institutions can grow more insecure without any open break in law.

Week 70 did not depend on one crisis. It deepened erosion through combination. Legal protection for the ruler, weaker voting safeguards, harsher status lines, donor-shaped access, sacred pageantry, and selective judicial rescue all appeared in the same span. The republic still showed signs of resistance. Yet more and more of that resistance was reactive, narrow, and forced to defend ground already lost. That is how a system changes before it admits that it has changed.
